endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Require vendors to provide subgroup performance data before contract execution rather than post-deployment.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether training frontline staff to escalate, halt, or roll back agentic AI actions reduces harm, and no supplied study documents how often staff fail to stop erroneous agent actions. The only endorsing source, a CHAI governance playbook, addresses pre-contract vendor subgroup performance data and does not speak to user training for stopping or reversing agent actions.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for R256 contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single endorsement comes from a framework rather than empirical work. Its quoted text concerns vendor subgroup data before contract execution, so it offers indirect support at most for a training recommendation.

The supplied material does not show how often staff are unable to stop or reverse agent actions, how severe the resulting harms are, or whether trained users intercept errors before they reach patients. Without hazard or intervention data, the size of the safety benefit from halt and rollback training remains unknown.

The CHAI playbook language supplied here sets an expectation that vendors disclose subgroup performance data before contracting. That expectation applies to procurement and does not establish a standard for frontline escalation, halt, or rollback training. Health systems adopting R256 would be acting without a directly matching endorsement in this evidence map.

commentary.research_gap: No study has measured whether trained frontline users halt or reverse erroneous agentic AI actions more often or more quickly than untrained users, or whether such training changes patient harm. Studies are also needed that document how often agent actions go unstopped in clinical workflows and whether systems provide working halt and rollback controls for training to build on.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study tested this practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. This means health systems serving these groups have no data on whether halt and rollback training works under their staffing levels and workflows.
